title: Thinking through Uncertainty: Nonconsequential Reasoning and Choice

source.title: Thinking through Uncertainty: Nonconsequential Reasoning and Choice

studies.title: Prisoner’s Dilemma · Known versus unknown move
Newcomb’s problem · One box or both
Reasoning tasks · Choosing what to inspect

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Can knowing an event’s outcome change a decision even when a person would make the same choice under either possible outcome?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: The strongest within-person evidence comes from Prisoner’s Dilemma games. The paper also reports Newcomb-style tasks and discusses conditional reasoning and prediction.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: Some people made one choice when the opponent’s move was unknown, even though they chose the opposite action after being told either possible move.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: If a person prefers an action under each known state, the same action should also be preferred without knowing which state obtains. The focal comparisons test departures from this principle.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: The paper’s disjunction account is a proposed explanation. A violation requires comparing the same person’s choices under both known cases and the uncertain case, not just aggregate percentages.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Eighty Princeton undergraduates made computer-based one-shot choices. Each focal game has an unknown-opponent version, then known-cooperate and known-compete versions in counterbalanced order.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: Some people competed after learning either possible opponent move yet cooperated when the move was unknown. The authors analyze these patterns at the level of individual game triads.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Forty participants from the game study face a bonus-point task with a predictor. They choose both boxes or the box whose contents depend on the prediction. Additional versions examine explicitly known versus unknown states.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The contrast illustrates how an uncertain state can elicit a choice different from the choices favored when the possible states are evaluated separately.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: The paper uses conditional-rule and prediction examples to explore where people may fail to think through both sides of a disjunction.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The authors relate these patterns to the experimental decision results. The examples should not all be read as independently randomized samples.
